stories.headline: NASDAQ-100 REBOUNDS 1.17% AS CHIPS LEAD AN AI-OPTIMISM BOUNCE
stories.body: The Nasdaq 100 climbed 1.17% to 29,529 and the S&P 500 added 0.41% to 7,691, clawing back a chunk of last week's AI-capex-driven selloff as Nvidia and chipmakers rallied on renewed optimism and earnings that beat lowered bars.
stories.explain: Because the Nasdaq 100 is cap-weighted, a handful of mega-cap chip and hyperscaler names rallying 2-4% can lift the whole index over a point even when breadth is unremarkable. Today's bounce reads less like a reversal of the underlying AI-capex-ROI doubts from last week than an oversold technical snapback: once short-term positioning gets this stretched, better-than-feared earnings from a couple of bellwethers are enough to trigger relief buying, even if the structural question about whether capex spending is matched by returns stays unresolved.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD TICKS UP TO 5.14% AS SUPPLY WEIGHS ON BONDS
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield rose 4 basis points to 5.14%, back above last week's peak, as this week's Treasury auction calendar and today's equity rally pulled money out of the safe-haven bid that had briefly capped yields.
stories.explain: When stocks are selling off, Treasuries attract a flight-to-quality bid that pushes yields down even if the macro backdrop argues for higher rates; today's rally reverses that flow, so some of the move is simply the safety premium coming back out of bonds. Layer on a heavy slate of new issuance this week and the government competing for the same pool of buyers, and yields drift higher on supply/demand mechanics alone. At 5.14%, the 10-year sits near multi-decade highs that directly raise the discount rate used to value every future cash flow, which is why equity valuations stay sensitive to every basis point here.

stories.headline: WTI CLIMBS TO $98 AS HORMUZ RISK PREMIUM PERSISTS
stories.body: WTI crude added 0.91% to $98 a barrel, holding onto most of last week's geopolitical-driven spike tied to tension around the Strait of Hormuz even as the most extreme pricing has started to unwind.
stories.explain: A risk premium tied to a shipping chokepoint gets built from war-risk insurance costs and options skew well before any barrel actually fails to move, so prices can stay elevated purely on the threat even without a realized supply disruption. That premium persisting at $98 rather than fully round-tripping back toward pre-spike levels signals traders still see the Hormuz risk as live rather than resolved, which keeps a floor under the price until there's a clear de-escalation headline.

stories.headline: GOLD RETREATS 0.97% TO $4,160 AS RISK APPETITE RETURNS
stories.body: Spot gold fell 0.97% to roughly $4,160 an ounce as today's equity rebound and a firmer dollar curbed demand for the metal as a defensive hedge.
stories.explain: Gold competes with Treasuries and cash as a place to park money, and it pays no yield, so when risk appetite returns and the dollar strengthens, the opportunity cost of holding bullion rises and some of that haven money rotates back into stocks or rate-bearing assets. The pullback also reflects today's bond weakness: gold often tracks real yields inversely, so a 10-year yield pushing back above 5.1% removes some of the relative appeal gold had when yields were capped by safe-haven flows.

stories.headline: DOLLAR FIRMS TO 101.97 AS RATE-DIFFERENTIAL TRADE REASSERTS
stories.body: The dollar index rose 0.15% to 101.97 as the greenback's yield advantage over the euro and yen reasserted itself alongside today's rise in Treasury yields.
stories.explain: The dollar index is a basket weighted roughly 58% to the euro and 14% to the yen, so it moves mainly on relative rate expectations between the Fed and the ECB or Bank of Japan. When U.S. yields rise faster than peers', as they did today with the 10-year up 4 bps, the carry advantage of holding dollar-denominated assets widens, and that pulls flows into the dollar almost mechanically, independent of any U.S.-specific news.

stories.headline: AP PRESEASON TOP 25 LOOMS AS FLORIDA, DUKE HEADLINE NO. 1 RACE
stories.body: With the men's regular season tipping off Nov. 2, the AP's preseason Top 25 is expected any day. Florida was tabbed No. 1 in the SEC's preseason media poll and is widely projected as Duke's closest rival for the national top spot; the two meet Dec. 1 in Gainesville as part of the ACC/SEC Challenge.

stories.headline: LAKERS' RECORD $12.5B SALE AWAITS LEAGUE VOTE AS SEASON OPENS TUESDAY
stories.body: The agreed sale of the Lakers to Bob Iger and Josh Kushner for a record $12.5 billion, topping last year's $10B Buss-to-Walter deal, still needs NBA Board of Governors approval next month, even as the 2026-27 season tips off Tuesday with a three-game opening slate led by Celtics at Pistons.

stories.headline: COMMANDERS AT 49ERS HEADLINE MNF AS TRADE FRENZY ROLLS ON
stories.body: San Francisco (5-0) hosts Washington (1-3-1) tonight on Monday Night Football, kickoff 8:15 PM ET/6:15 PM MT, with the Commanders 0-2 on the road this year against a Niners team that's 3-0 at home. The game is still to be played; it caps a week in which J.J. McCarthy, Joey Porter Jr. and Cam Jurgens all switched teams ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline.

stories.headline: WEEK 7'S UPSETS RESHAPE THE PLAYOFF PICTURE HEADING INTO WEEK 8
stories.body: Saturday's chaos, BYU's 28-24 stunner over Notre Dame, Ohio State's shaky 19-15 escape past Indiana (losing QB Julian Sayin to injury), Florida's comeback past Texas, and Tennessee's rout of Alabama, has scrambled the committee picture with the AP's updated Top 25 still digesting the results.

deepDive.title: How AI Capex Debt Is Turning a Tech Story Into a Credit Story
content: Today's bounce, the Nasdaq 100 up 1.17% to 29,529, reads as relief after last week's AI-capex-driven selloff, but the relief is narrower than the headline number suggests. The underlying worry was never just whether AI spending is too aggressive; it's whether that spending is increasingly financed with debt rather than free cash flow. A hyperscaler funding a data center out of operating cash flow is a capital-allocation question. The same hyperscaler funding it by issuing investment-grade bonds, or routing it through an off-balance-sheet joint venture, is a leverage question, and leverage questions get priced in the bond market before they show up in the stock.

The mechanism is straightforward once you separate the two financing paths. When a company spends from cash flow, a disappointing return on that capex shows up as a lower ROIC and a multiple compression, painful but contained. When the same spend is debt-funded, a disappointing return also raises leverage ratios and can pressure the credit rating, which widens the spread investors demand to hold that company's bonds. Wider spreads raise the cost of the next round of borrowing, which is exactly the dynamic now showing up as hyperscaler capex runs near an estimated $400 billion annualized pace for 2026, with a growing share routed through debt-financed vehicles rather than paid for outright.

What most people watching the stock price miss is that credit spreads tend to move first. The closest historical parallel is the late-1990s telecom buildout, when carriers like WorldCom and Global Crossing issued tens of billions in bonds to lay fiber ahead of demand that never fully materialized. Telecom bond spreads began widening noticeably in 2000, a full year before the equity collapse that followed in 2001-02, because bondholders were pricing the leverage mismatch well before equity investors gave up on the growth story. The lesson isn't that AI capex will fail the same way; it's that the credit market is the earlier, more honest read on whether the spending is sustainable.

That's the lens worth applying to today's setup: a 10-year yield at 5.14% already raises the bar for any debt-funded project to clear, since the risk-free rate against which corporate borrowing is priced keeps climbing. Chris's practical takeaway is to watch investment-grade spreads on megacap tech issuers alongside the equity tape, not instead of it, over the next few weeks. If spreads stay tight even as the 10-year grinds higher, the market is still underwriting the AI capex cycle. If they start widening before the Nov. 10 CPI print or the Fed's Dec. 9 decision, that's the credit market signaling a leverage problem well before it shows up in anyone's earnings call.
